title: Everyday Laws Everyone Should Know
summary: Ten legal rules and golden rules that keep you safe in daily life.

body.text: You do not need to be a lawyer to stay out of trouble. A few basic legal ideas cover most of what happens in daily life.

items: Constitution: every person has Fundamental Rights - equality before the law, freedom of speech, and protection of life and personal freedom. If the government breaks these, courts can cancel its action.

Criminal law: an offence is a wrong that the law punishes; a complaint is the written information you give the police; an FIR is the first formal record of a cognisable offence (a serious crime the police must act on); an arrest means being taken into custody; a court case decides if someone is guilty. If you know which is which, you will not panic.
Evidence: what you keep decides what you can prove. Save messages, emails, receipts, photos, and CCTV details. Collect them in a lawful way.
Public behaviour: too much noise, public nuisance, trespassing (entering a place without permission), assault, and damaging property can all lead to punishment, even if they seem small.
Privacy: protect your Aadhaar, PAN, bank details, and personal photos. If you share them carelessly, you may face fraud or blackmail.
Women's safety: the law protects against stalking, harassment, domestic violence, and sexual harassment at work.
Child protection: child labour is restricted. Children also have special protection against sexual offences under the POCSO Act.
Taxes: learn your income tax basics - Form 16, AIS, TDS, and when you must file a return.
Agreements: before you sign, read the payment terms, penalties, and termination (ending) clauses. What you sign binds you.
Civic duties: follow waste-disposal rules, protect public property, and obey local rules. These are legal duties, not just good manners.
Never sign a paper you have not read or understood.
Never share an OTP, UPI PIN, or bank password with anyone.
Keep copies of job contracts, loan agreements, receipts, and important letters.
If the police or another authority contacts you, stay calm. Cooperate in a lawful way. If you do not understand what is happening, ask them to explain.
If someone threatens you, do not make the situation worse. Save the evidence and get the right help.
Never ignore a court summons, legal notice, or official deadline without knowing what it can lead to.
Check legal claims on official government websites. Do not trust viral social-media videos.
For a serious legal problem, ask a qualified lawyer. Do not depend only on general information from the internet.

body.text: Not every right is unlimited. Many rights have reasonable limits. The exact rule can depend on your state and on the facts of your case.
If you are not sure, keep the paper and ask for it in writing. A written record is much stronger than memory.
The three new criminal laws (from 1 July 2024)

items: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita: deals with offences.
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita: deals with procedure.
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam: deals with evidence.
All three came into force on 1 July 2024.
Respect the Constitution.
Protect public property.
Promote harmony.
Rights are not absolute.
Reasonable restrictions apply.
Keep your documents.
Always ask for reasons in writing.

practicalSteps: Save 112, 1930, 1915 and 15100 in your phone today.
Keep a folder (on paper or online) of your important documents and receipts.
Before you sign anything, ask for a copy and time to read it.
Whenever something happens, note the date, names, and reference numbers.
exceptions: Fundamental Rights mostly apply against the State (the government). A few also apply to private persons.
A declared emergency can limit some rights. But Articles 20 and 21 cannot be stopped.

faqs.q: If I do not know the law, am I excused?
faqs.a: Usually no. Not knowing the law is rarely a defence. That is exactly why these basics matter.

faqs.q: How do I check if a legal claim is true?
faqs.a: Use official sources - India Code, the department website, and the specific Act. Not forwarded messages or short videos.

misconceptions.fact: Most rights have reasonable limits. The exact limit depends on the law and the facts.
